name: Rigwe

catalog_citation: Gya, Daniel & Roger Blench. 2008. Phonology of the Rigwe language. Draft circulated for comment (printout 19 January 2008), 31 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (unpublished; Glottolog ref 435429). the Internet Archive capture of rogerblench.info/Language/Niger-Congo/BC/Plateau/Rigwe/Grammar/Rigwe.
catalog_locator: Section 3 'Tone', printed pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 29-30); tone-marking table also in section 2.1, printed p. 1 (PDF p. 3). File: the copy we hold.
catalog_quote: Rigwe has four tones and at least two falling glide tones; High ˊ / Mid Unmarked / Mid over a syllabic nasal ¯ / Low ˋ / Extra-Low ˵ / Falling ^ / High-mid fall ᷇ There are apparently no rising tones. Four-way contrasts are rare but the following example shows a contrastive set on a CV syllable; tá leg / ta to arrange / tà place of lower altitude / tȁ belt. In connected speech, extra low tone is raised to low, but normal low and extra low tone are easily distinguished in plural formations. ... Extra low becomes Low in a sentence context. ... Most cases of falling tone are High-Low. However, the tone on some word-final velar nasals is High-Mid ( ᷇) in sentence context. ... There appear to be no true rising tones in Rigwe although they can occur phonetically as a consequence of a sequence of two identical vowels.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rigwe is described purely as a tone language with four contrastive level tones (H, M, L, extra-L) and falling contours; the only dedicated phonology of the language contains no statement at all about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be assigned from the primary literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: extra-low is realised as low in sentence context; some word-final velar nasals carry a High-Mid fall; phonetic rises only across VV sequences or CVŋ after pronoun tone perturbation.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement covers citation forms and connected speech (sandhi noted); nothing on word- or phrase-level stress/prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Rigwe (Irigwe, iso iri = irig1241) as spoken in Miango and Kwall, Bassa LGA, Plateau State; the authors note very little dialect variation, so no sub-variety issue. 'Rigwe' is the authors' preferred name for the same language.

sources.note: Nothing. Section 3 'Tone' (pp. 27-28) describes four level tones (High, Mid, Low, Extra-Low) plus falling glides (HL, H-M), no rising tones, sandhi (extra-low -> low in sentence context, tone perturbation on pronouns); vowels section treats doubled vowels as VV sequences bearing distinct tones. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the 31 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent/promin/rhythm/weight: 0 hits).
